opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think that's one of the most fun parts of doing research this way. With the Continuous Thought Machine, we didn't set out with a checklist of "it needs to do X, Y, and Z." The starting point was much more of a hunch: neural networks threw away something important when we abstracted the neuron down to a simple activation function, and that something is time. Real neurons have dynamics, and the timing between them seems to matter. So we asked, what if we put that back in? Give each neuron a little bit of its own history to work with, and use the synchronization between neurons as the actual representation.

Once you build something like that and start playing with it, it starts showing you things you didn't expect. You give it a maze, and it looks like it's tracing out a path while it thinks. It takes more internal steps on harder examples and fewer on easy ones, and we never explicitly told it to do that adaptive compute thing. It just fell out of the design. When that happens, the worst thing you can do is say, "That's not what this project is about, let's get back to beating the benchmark."

So my approach is to give myself, and the team, permission to follow those threads. A lot of the field right now is very hill-climbing. You pick a leaderboard, you tweak things, you squeeze out half a percent. That's useful work, but it's not where the genuinely new ideas come from. With the transformer, a lot of what made it important wasn't obvious at the time. We were doing translation. Nobody in that room was thinking, "This is going to be the thing for language models, images, proteins, everything." The interesting properties were discovered by people poking at it.

So when the architecture opens up something unexpected, I treat that as the signal, not the noise. You don't want to over-commit too early, either. You want to explore broadly, see which of these surprising behaviours are robust, and then decide where to dig deep. It's a bit like evolution: you want a lot of variation, and you let the interesting stuff reveal itself, rather than deciding up front exactly what the endpoint should look like.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we didn't actually set out with the continuous thought machine to build something that did all the things it ended up doing. It started from a fairly simple frustration, which is that modern neural networks have thrown away almost everything about how neurons actually behave over time. We flatten activity into a single number, we drop the temporal dynamics, we don't use synchronization at all, and we did that for good engineering reasons, but it always bothered me that the one thing we know produces intelligence, which is the brain, does something quite different.

So at Sakana we tried to put some of that back in. Give neurons their own little history, let them operate over an internal time dimension that's decoupled from the data, and use the synchronization between neurons as the actual representation. And then the interesting thing is what happens once you've done that. You start seeing behaviors you didn't engineer. The model takes longer to think about harder problems. It develops something that looks like attention wandering over an image. It can solve mazes it wasn't really trained on at that length. And none of that was in the original plan.

My approach to that, I guess, is to be quite deliberate about not over-steering. The temptation when something surprising shows up is to immediately pivot and optimize for it and turn it into a benchmark number, and I think that kills a lot of research. If you look at the transformer, honestly, a lot of what made it useful was stuff we didn't anticipate either. We were just trying to get rid of recurrence to make translation train faster. So I've learned to treat those unexpected properties as the signal that you're near something real, rather than as a distraction from the plan.

Practically what that means is we try to keep the team small, we run a lot of small experiments, and we spend time just looking at what the model does rather than only looking at loss curves. If the architecture is doing something weird, we try to understand why before we decide whether to chase it. And I try to resist the pressure to justify everything in terms of beating a leaderboard, because the stuff I'm most excited about right now, which is whether these dynamics give you adaptive compute or emergent reasoning, you can't really measure with the existing benchmarks anyway. So the research question kind of has to lead, and the architecture tells you where to look.

r002.rationale: It presents the brain-inspired architecture as a way to uncover unanticipated behaviors and investigate emergent reasoning, including solving mazes beyond the training setup.

r003.rationale: It raises research questions about adaptive compute and emergent reasoning, but does not propose using emergent problem-solving approaches to formulate philosophical questions about intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be willing to let the thing surprise you. You start with an intuition—perhaps there’s something useful about giving a model time to work through a problem—but that intuition isn’t a specification of everything the model ought to do. Once you build it, the interesting question becomes: what is it actually doing, and which of those behaviours are worth understanding?

With something like the continuous thought machine, I’d treat the brain inspiration as a source of ideas, rather than a requirement to reproduce the brain. You still need experiments that tell you whether a particular mechanism is helping. Can you remove it? Can you simplify it? Does the behaviour persist across different tasks?

And then you need a bit of freedom to follow the unexpected result. If you only pursue the outcome you originally wrote down, you can miss the most interesting part of the research. The trick is to stay open about where you’re going while being quite strict about the evidence that takes you there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be willing to let the research change the question. You start with an intuition—perhaps there’s something useful about giving a network its own internal dynamics—but that intuition isn’t a guarantee that the particular thing you imagined will work. You build it, look at what it actually does, and then decide which observations deserve another experiment.

With something like the continuous thought machine, the brain inspiration gives you a starting point. It doesn’t settle the engineering questions. If an unexpected behaviour opens up a direction we hadn’t considered, I’d want to follow it, but also try to isolate what’s causing it. Is it a useful consequence of the architecture? Does it persist when we change the task? Can we remove a component and still get the same effect?

So there’s a balance between having enough conviction to explore an unusual idea and not becoming attached to your original explanation of why it should work. The interesting result might turn out to be somewhere else.
